## Part 3 - Writer Verification using a Siamese Network

### Objective

The aim of this task is to determine whether two handwriting images were written by the same person.

Unlike the CNN in Task 2, which predicts one of 20 writers, the Siamese network learns a similarity function. Given two images, the network outputs the probability that both images belong to the same writer.

This transforms writer identification into a binary classification problem:

Same writer = 1; Different writer = 0

#### Step 1 - Create training and testing sets

To check whether the model could recognise a writer's handwriting in a new session, we trained it on images from Sessions 1-3, validated on images from session 3 and tested it on images from Session 5. This showed whether the model could identify the same writer from handwriting samples it had never seen before. This avoids information leakage and creates a realistic evaluation framework.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

metadata <- data$metadata

# Training images
train_idx <- which(metadata$session %in% c(1,2,3))

#Validation images
validation_idx <- which(metadata$session == 4)

# Test images
test_idx <- which(metadata$session == 5)

train_meta <- metadata[train_idx,]
validation_meta <- metadata[validation_idx,]
test_meta <- metadata[test_idx,]

```

#### Step 2 - Construct Positive and Negative Pairs

The Siamese network was trained using pairs of handwriting images. Pairs containing two samples from the same writer were labelled as **1**, while pairs containing samples from different writers were labelled as **0**. By learning from these pairs, the model focused on identifying how similar two handwriting samples were, rather than learning to recognise specific writers directly.

```{r}
#Positive Pair Function
set.seed(20260923)
create_positive_pairs <- function(meta,
                                  pairs_per_group = 200)
{
  pairs <- list()
  counter <- 1
  
  for(writer in unique(meta$person_id))
  {
    for(d in unique(meta$digit))
    {
      idx <- which(meta$person_id == writer & meta$digit == d)
      
      if(length(idx) < 2)
        next
      
      n_possible <- choose(length(idx), 2)
      
      n_pairs <- min(pairs_per_group,
                     n_possible)
      
      pair_mat <- replicate(n_pairs,
                            sample(idx, 2, replace = FALSE))
      
      pairs[[counter]] <- data.frame(img1 = pair_mat[1, ],
                                     img2 = pair_mat[2, ],
                                     label = 1)
      
      counter <- counter + 1
    }
  }
  
  bind_rows(pairs)
}

#Negative Pair Function
create_negative_pairs <- function(meta, n_pairs)
{
  img1_vec <- integer(n_pairs)
  img2_vec <- integer(n_pairs)
  
  pair_set <- new.env(hash = TRUE)
  
  count <- 0
  
  while(count < n_pairs)
  {
    img1 <- sample(nrow(meta), 1)
    
    writer1 <- meta$person_id[img1]
    digit1 <- meta$digit[img1]
    
    candidates <- which(meta$person_id != writer1 & meta$digit == digit1)
    
    if(length(candidates) == 0)
      next
    
    img2 <- sample(candidates, 1)
    
    key <- paste(min(img1,img2),
                 max(img1,img2),
                 sep = "_")
    
    if(exists(key, envir = pair_set))
      next
    
    count <- count + 1
    
    img1_vec[count] <- img1
    img2_vec[count] <- img2
    
    assign(key, TRUE, envir = pair_set)
  }
  
  data.frame(
    img1 = img1_vec,
    img2 = img2_vec,
    label = 0
  )
}
  
#Create Training Pairs
train_positive <- create_positive_pairs(train_meta, pairs_per_group = 200)

train_negative <- create_negative_pairs(train_meta, 
                                        nrow(train_positive))

train_pairs <- rbind(train_positive, train_negative)

#Create Validation Pairs
validation_positive <- create_positive_pairs(validation_meta)

validation_negative <- create_negative_pairs(validation_meta, 
                                        nrow(validation_positive))

validation_pairs <- rbind(validation_positive, validation_negative)

#Create Test Pairs
test_positive <- create_positive_pairs(test_meta)

test_negative <- create_negative_pairs(test_meta,
                                       nrow(test_positive))

test_pairs <- rbind(test_positive, test_negative)

```

#### Step 3 - Create Siamese Inputs

Keras requires two input arrays: Input A and Input B; and one output: Same writer?

```{r}
#Training images:
set.seed(20260923)
train_images <- data$images[train_idx,,,, drop = FALSE]
validation_images  <- data$images[validation_idx,,,, drop = FALSE]
test_images  <- data$images[test_idx,,,, drop = FALSE]

# Normalise
train_images <- train_images / 255
validation_images  <- validation_images / 255
test_images  <- test_images / 255

#dim(train_images)
#dim(test_images)

#Build Pair Arrays
build_pair_arrays <- function(images, pairs)
{
  x1 <- images[pairs$img1,,,, drop = FALSE]
  x2 <- images[pairs$img2,,,, drop = FALSE]
  
  y <- pairs$label
  
  list(x1 = x1,
       x2 = x2,
       y = y)
}

train_data_pairs <- build_pair_arrays(train_images, train_pairs)
validation_data_pairs <- build_pair_arrays(validation_images, validation_pairs)
test_data_pairs <- build_pair_arrays(test_images, test_pairs)

```

#### Step 4 - Build the Siamese Network

Both branches use exactly the same CNN.

The encoder learns writer-specific features such as:

stroke thickness, digit shape, slant, curvature and spacing patterns

The network then compares feature representations.

```{r}
#Encoder
#install.packages("keras3")
library(keras3)
library(reticulate)
set.seed(20260923)
py_require("tensorflow")
use_backend("tensorflow")
tensorflow::tf_version()

# Shared Encoder
encoder <- create_encoder()

input_a <- layer_input(shape = c(28,28,1))
input_b <- layer_input(shape = c(28,28,1))

encoded_a <- encoder(input_a)
encoded_b <- encoder(input_b)

# Euclidean Distance Function
euclidean_distance <- function(vectors)
{
  x <- vectors[[1]]
  y <- vectors[[2]]
  
  op_sqrt(op_sum(op_square(x - y),
                 axis = -1,
                 keepdims = TRUE))
}

# Distance Layer
distance <- layer_lambda(list(encoded_a, encoded_b),
                         euclidean_distance)

# Create Siamese Model
siamese_model <- keras_model(inputs = list(input_a, input_b),
                             outputs = distance)

# Contrastive Loss
contrastive_loss <- function(y_true, y_pred)
{
  margin <- 1
  
  op_mean(y_true * op_square(y_pred) + (1 - y_true) *
            op_square(op_maximum(margin - y_pred, 0)))
}

# Compile Model
siamese_model |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(),
                         loss = contrastive_loss)

# View architecture
summary(siamese_model)

#dim(train_data_pairs$x1)
#dim(train_data_pairs$x2)
#length(train_data_pairs$y)
```

#### Step 5 - Train The Model

```{r}
#train the model
set.seed(20260923)
options(keras.view_metrics = FALSE)

history <- siamese_model |> 
  fit(x = list(train_data_pairs$x1,train_data_pairs$x2),
      y = train_data_pairs$y,
      validation_data = list(list(validation_data_pairs$x1,
                                  validation_data_pairs$x2),
                             validation_data_pairs$y),
      epochs = 10,
      batch_size = 64)

plot(history)

#table(train_data_pairs$y)

```

The graph shows:

- **Training loss (red)** decreases steadily from about **0.046** to **0.007**.

<!-- -->

- **Validation loss (blue)** decreases from about **0.027** to **0.022** during the first few epochs.

<!-- -->

- After around **Epoch 6**, the validation loss stops improving and becomes almost flat, with a very slight increase near the end.

The graph shows the training and validation loss during model training. Both losses decreased during the first few epochs, indicating that the Siamese network was learning meaningful writer-specific features. The validation loss reached its lowest value at approximately Epoch 6 and then remained relatively stable, while the training loss continued to decrease. This suggests mild overfitting in later epochs, although the small gap between the training and validation losses indicates that the model maintained good generalisation performance.

#### Step 6 - Evaluate The Model

The Siamese network produces a distance score instead of directly predicting whether two images were written by the same person. A threshold was chosen using the validation data. If the distance between two images was below the threshold, they were classified as being written by the same writer. If the distance was above the threshold, they were classified as being written by different writers. Several threshold values were tested, and the one with the highest balanced accuracy was selected. This threshold was then used to evaluate the model on the test set.

```{r}
library(caret)
set.seed(20260923)

# Predict distances on validation set
val_distances <- as.numeric(predict(siamese_model,
                         list(validation_data_pairs$x1,
                              validation_data_pairs$x2)))

valid_same <- validation_data_pairs$y == 1

balanced_accuracy_at <- function(cut)
{
  predicts_same <- val_distances < cut
  
  same_rate <- mean(predicts_same[valid_same])
  
  different_rate <- mean(!predicts_same[!valid_same])
  
  (same_rate + different_rate) / 2
}

threshold_candidates <- sort(unique(val_distances))

threshold_scores <- vapply(threshold_candidates,
                           balanced_accuracy_at,
                           numeric(1))

best_index <- which.max(threshold_scores)

best_threshold <- threshold_candidates[best_index]
best_threshold

max_balanced_accuracy <- threshold_scores[best_index]
max_balanced_accuracy

#summary(val_distances)
#min(val_distances)
#max(val_distances)



```

something

```{r}
#Predict distances on test set
set.seed(20260923)
pred_distances <- predict(siamese_model,
                          list(test_data_pairs$x1,
                               test_data_pairs$x2))

#Convert distances into same/different writer predictions:
#threshold <- 0.5

pred_class <- ifelse(pred_distances < best_threshold, 1, 0)

cm <- confusionMatrix(factor(pred_class),
                      factor(test_data_pairs$y, levels = c(0, 1)),
                      positive = "1")

cm

accuracy <- cm$overall["Accuracy"]

precision <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]

recall <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]

specificity <- cm$byClass["Specificity"]

f1_score <- 2 * (precision * recall) /
  (precision + recall)

data.frame(Accuracy = accuracy,
           Precision = precision,
           Recall = recall,
           Specificity = specificity,
           F1_Score = f1_score)

library(pROC)

roc_obj <- roc(response = test_data_pairs$y,
               predictor = as.vector(-pred_distances))

plot(roc_obj,
     col = "blue",
     main = "ROC Curve")

auc(roc_obj)
```
